# GPT-4 vs Claude — Summarization Comparison

**Task:** Summarize the key points of the article about renewable energy advancements (2024 overview).
**Materials reviewed:** `article.txt`, `gpt4_answer.txt`, `claude_answer.txt`

A note on method: per the LLM-evaluation framework, I assessed both answers across the core dimensions (accuracy, coverage/fidelity, specificity, conciseness, fluency, structure). Automated metric computation (ROUGE/BLEU/BERTScore) could not be executed in this session, so the evaluation below is a manual, source-grounded review with a term-coverage check against the article.

---

## 1. Summary of Each Answer

| | **GPT-4** | **Claude** |
|---|---|---|
| Length | ~120 words, bullet format | ~230 words, narrative paragraphs |
| Style | Informal, high-level ("growing a lot", "pretty cheap", "Lots of money") | Professional, dense, well-organized |
| Specific facts | **0** numbers, **0** named entities | ~20+ quantitative facts and named projects retained |
| Accuracy | All statements true, but trivially so | Faithful to source; no hallucinations or distortions |

## 2. Coverage Check (key content from the article)

**Key article facts:** 33.7% tandem-cell efficiency; 20% cost cut by 2026; China at 80% of manufacturing; IRA's $50B; floating solar (10–15% gain); Dogger Bank 3.6 GW; 15 MW/260 m turbines; $50–60/MWh offshore cost; 150 GWh storage (300% increase); LFP replacing NMC; sodium-ion; iron-air (100-hr); hydrogen at $3–4/kg vs. $2/kg target; steel/shipping applications; $500B investment; 14M jobs (40M projected); carbon pricing covering 23%; grid/permitting/supply-chain challenges; intermittency vs. baseload debate; 2050 net-zero.

| Article element | GPT-4 | Claude |
|---|---|---|
| Efficiency gains (perovskite, 33.7%) | "getting more efficient" (no figure) | ✅ 33.7%, cost −20% by 2026 |
| Manufacturing (China 80%, IRA $50B) | "China makes most of them" | ✅ 80%, US/India/EU, IRA $50B |
| Floating solar | ✅ "float on water" (no 10–15% stat) | ❌ omitted |
| Offshore wind / Dogger Bank | "especially offshore" (no specifics) | ✅ Dogger Bank 3.6 GW |
| Turbine specs & costs | "getting bigger" / "pretty cheap" | ✅ 15 MW, 260 m rotors, $50–60/MWh |
| Storage (150 GWh, LFP, sodium-ion, iron-air) | "increasing" / "new types" | ✅ 150 GWh, LFP→NMC, sodium-ion, iron-air |
| Hydrogen ($3–4/kg, steel/shipping) | "becoming cheaper", "used in industry" | ✅ $3–4/kg, steel + shipping |
| Investment/jobs/carbon pricing | "lots of money", "many jobs" | ✅ $500B, 14M jobs, 23% coverage |
| Challenges (grid, permitting, minerals, intermittency) | "grid infrastructure needs work" | ✅ grid, permitting, supply chains, baseload debate |
| 2050 net-zero outlook | "more work is needed" | ✅ 2050 net-zero framing |

**Fidelity estimate:** GPT-4 retains ~5 of the article's ~25 concrete facts (≈20%); Claude retains ~22 (≈85–90%).

## 3. Dimension-by-Dimension Ratings

| Dimension | GPT-4 | Claude | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Accuracy / groundedness | 8/10 | 9/10 | Both hallucination-free; Claude's specifics match the source exactly |
| Coverage / recall of key points | 5/10 | 9/10 | GPT-4 covers categories only; Claude preserves the article's substance |
| Specificity / information density | 4/10 | 9/10 | GPT-4 contains zero figures or named entities |
| Conciseness | 9/10 | 7/10 | GPT-4 is tighter; Claude's extra length is justified by content |
| Fluency / clarity | 7/10 | 9/10 | Both clear; GPT-4's informal register undersells the material |
| Structure / organization | 7/10 | 9/10 | Bullets vs. coherent narrative with logical progression |

## 4. Strengths & Weaknesses

**GPT-4**
- ✅ Readable, scannable, safe; would suit a casual audience
- ✅ No factual errors or unsupported claims
- ❌ Drops virtually all quantitative and technical content — the actual "key points" of this article
- ❌ Informal tone ("Lots of money", "pretty cheap") is a poor fit for a technical-summarization task
- ❌ Misses the challenges/intermittency nuance beyond a generic nod

**Claude**
- ✅ Preserves the article's analytical value: efficiency milestones, costs, named projects (Dogger Bank), chemistry shifts (NMC→LFP, sodium-ion), and the policy landscape (IRA, carbon pricing)
- ✅ Correctly balances progress vs. remaining challenges and keeps the net-zero framing
- ✅ Professional register matching the source material
- ❌ Minor omissions: floating solar, onshore wind costs ($30–40/MWh), compressed-air/gravity storage, CBAM, the 40M jobs projection
- ❌ Slightly longer, so marginally less scannable

## 5. Verdict

**Claude produces the better summary for this task.** "Key points" of a data-dense 2024 industry overview requires retaining the specifics — efficiency figures, cost curves, capacity numbers, named technologies, and policy drivers — and Claude does this with high fidelity, accuracy, and an appropriate register. GPT-4's answer is competent and error-free as a *topic overview*, but it abstracts away nearly all the article's substance, making it substantially less useful as a summary of *key points*.

**Recommendation:** Adopt Claude's output for this task. If only one answer can be used, GPT-4's would serve only as a lightweight executive teaser, not the substantive summary. If this were a live evaluation pipeline, I'd next (a) run ROUGE-1/ROUGE-L and BERTScore against a reference summary, (b) add an LLM-as-judge pairwise pass for confirmation, and (c) add a groundedness check to guard against future hallucinations.

Renewable Energy Advancements: A 2024 Overview

The renewable energy sector has experienced remarkable growth and technological breakthroughs in 2024, fundamentally reshaping the global energy landscape. This article examines the key developments across solar, wind, battery storage, and emerging technologies.

Solar Power Innovations

Solar panel efficiency has reached new heights, with perovskite-silicon tandem cells achieving 33.7% efficiency in commercial applications, up from 29% just two years ago. This breakthrough, pioneered by researchers at Oxford PV and NREL, promises to reduce the cost per watt by an additional 20% by 2026.

China continues to dominate solar manufacturing, producing 80% of global panels, but new facilities in the United States, India, and the European Union are diversifying supply chains. The U.S. Inflation Reduction Act has catalyzed $50 billion in domestic solar manufacturing investments.

Floating solar installations have emerged as a significant trend, with projects in Japan, South Korea, and the Netherlands demonstrating that water-based arrays can generate 10-15% more electricity than land-based equivalents due to the cooling effect of water.

Wind Energy Developments

Offshore wind has become the fastest-growing segment, with global capacity expected to triple by 2030. The Dogger Bank Wind Farm in the UK, now operational, generates 3.6 GW - enough to power 6 million homes.

Turbine technology has advanced significantly. The latest generation of offshore turbines features 15-megawatt capacity with 260-meter rotor diameters. GE's Haliade-X and Siemens Gamesa's SG 14-236 DD represent the cutting edge, reducing the levelized cost of offshore wind energy to $50-60 per megawatt-hour.

Onshore wind remains cost-competitive at $30-40/MWh in optimal locations, making it one of the cheapest electricity sources available. However, grid integration challenges and local opposition continue to slow deployment in some regions.

Battery Storage Revolution

Grid-scale battery storage has transformed from niche to necessity. Global installed capacity reached 150 GWh in 2024, a 300% increase from 2021. Lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries have largely replaced nickel-manganese-cobalt (NMC) chemistries for stationary storage due to lower cost, longer lifespan, and improved safety.

The emergence of sodium-ion batteries offers a promising alternative that eliminates dependence on lithium and cobalt. CATL and BYD have begun commercial production, with costs projected to fall below $80/kWh by 2026.

Long-duration energy storage solutions are advancing rapidly. Iron-air batteries from Form Energy promise 100-hour storage at costs competitive with natural gas peaker plants. Meanwhile, compressed air and gravity-based systems are finding niche applications.

Green Hydrogen Progress

Green hydrogen production costs have fallen to $3-4 per kilogram in optimal locations, approaching the $2/kg target needed for widespread industrial adoption. Major projects in Australia, Chile, and Saudi Arabia are scaling electrolysis capacity.

The technology is finding applications in steel production, shipping fuel, and seasonal energy storage. ThyssenKrupp's hydrogen-based steel production in Germany and Maersk's methanol-powered container ships represent early industrial adoption.

Policy and Investment Landscape

Global renewable energy investment reached $500 billion in 2024, with China, the United States, and the European Union leading deployment. The energy transition has created 14 million jobs worldwide, with projections suggesting 40 million by 2030.

Carbon pricing mechanisms now cover 23% of global emissions, up from 15% in 2020. The EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) is pressuring trading partners to adopt similar measures.

Challenges Remain

Despite progress, significant challenges persist. Grid infrastructure requires massive upgrades to handle variable renewable generation. Permitting delays add 2-4 years to project timelines in many jurisdictions. Critical mineral supply chains remain concentrated and vulnerable to disruption.

The intermittency challenge requires continued innovation in storage, demand response, and grid flexibility. Nuclear power advocates argue that baseload capacity remains essential, while renewables proponents point to declining costs and improving storage as sufficient solutions.

Conclusion

The renewable energy sector in 2024 demonstrates that the energy transition is accelerating beyond most projections. Technological innovation, supportive policies, and economic competitiveness are driving unprecedented deployment. However, achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 will require sustained investment, policy commitment, and continued technological advancement across all sectors of the economy.

"""Compare GPT-4 vs Claude summaries of article.txt.

Implements (pure Python, no external deps):
  - ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, ROUGE-L (precision / recall / F1) vs. source article
  - BLEU-1..4 with brevity penalty (lexical overlap with source)
  - Custom fact-retention metric: 23 key quantitative facts from the article
  - Length / compression ratio
  - Readability (Flesch Reading Ease, Flesch-Kincaid grade) -- descriptive only
"""
import math
import re
import string
from collections import Counter

PATHS = {"article": "article.txt", "gpt4": "gpt4_answer.txt", "claude": "claude_answer.txt"}

# --- Fact-retention checklist (from the article) ---------------------------
# Each fact has one or more alternative requirement sets; a fact is covered if
# ANY alternative's substrings all appear in the normalized summary text.
FACTS = [
    ("Perovskite-silicon tandem cells 33.7% efficiency",          [["33.7"]]),
    ("Efficiency up from 29% two years ago",                      [["29%"]]),
    ("20% cost-per-watt reduction by 2026",                       [["20% by 2026"]]),
    ("China produces 80% of panels",                              [["80%"]]),
    ("IRA catalyzed $50B in US solar manufacturing",              [["$50 billion"]]),
    ("Floating solar 10-15% more output",                         [["floating", "10-15%"]]),
    ("Dogger Bank 3.6 GW offshore farm",                          [["dogger bank", "3.6"]]),
    ("Powers 6 million homes",                                    [["6 million"]]),
    ("15 MW offshore turbines",                                   [["15 mw"]]),
    ("260-meter rotor diameters",                                 [["260"]]),
    ("Offshore wind cost $50-60/MWh",                             [["$50-60"]]),
    ("Onshore wind cost $30-40/MWh",                              [["$30-40"]]),
    ("Battery capacity 150 GWh, +300% (tripling) since 2021",     [["150 gwh", "300%"], ["150 gwh", "tripl"]]),
    ("LFP chemistry replacing NMC",                               [["lfp", "nmc"]]),
    ("Sodium-ion batteries emerging",                             [["sodium-ion"]]),
    ("Iron-air 100-hour long-duration storage",                   [["iron-air"]]),
    ("Green hydrogen cost $3-4/kg",                               [["$3-4"]]),
    ("$2/kg hydrogen cost target",                                [["$2"]]),
    ("$500B global investment",                                   [["$500 billion"]]),
    ("14 million jobs created",                                   [["14 million"]]),
    ("40 million jobs projected by 2030",                         [["40 million"]]),
    ("Carbon pricing covers 23% of emissions",                    [["23%"]]),
    ("Permitting delays of 2-4 years",                            [["2-4 years"]]),
]

TOPICS = ["solar", "wind", "battery", "hydrogen", "investment", "challenge", "storage", "policy"]

# --- Helpers ---------------------------------------------------------------
def read(p):
    with open(p, encoding="utf-8") as f:
        return f.read().strip()

def tokenize(text):
    toks = []
    for t in text.split():
        t = t.strip(string.punctuation)
        if t:
            toks.append(t.lower())
    return toks

def normalize(text):
    return re.sub(r"\s+", " ", text.lower())

def ngrams(tokens, n):
    if len(tokens) < n:
        return Counter()
    return Counter(zip(*(tokens[i:] for i in range(n))))

def rouge_n(ref_tokens, hyp_tokens, n):
    ref_ng, hyp_ng = ngrams(ref_tokens, n), ngrams(hyp_tokens, n)
    clipped = sum(min(c, ref_ng.get(g, 0)) for g, c in hyp_ng.items())
    ref_total, hyp_total = sum(ref_ng.values()), sum(hyp_ng.values())
    if ref_total == 0 or hyp_total == 0:
        return 0.0, 0.0, 0.0
    rec = clipped / ref_total
    prec = clipped / hyp_total
    f1 = 2 * prec * rec / (prec + rec) if (prec + rec) else 0.0
    return rec, prec, f1

def lcs_len(a, b):
    m, n = len(a), len(b)
    prev = [0] * (n + 1)
    for i in range(1, m + 1):
        cur = [0] * (n + 1)
        for j in range(1, n + 1):
            if a[i - 1] == b[j - 1]:
                cur[j] = prev[j - 1] + 1
            else:
                cur[j] = max(prev[j], cur[j - 1])
        prev = cur
    return prev[n]

def rouge_l(ref_tokens, hyp_tokens):
    lcs = lcs_len(ref_tokens, hyp_tokens)
    if not ref_tokens or not hyp_tokens:
        return 0.0, 0.0, 0.0
    rec = lcs / len(ref_tokens)
    prec = lcs / len(hyp_tokens)
    f1 = 2 * prec * rec / (prec + rec) if (prec + rec) else 0.0
    return rec, prec, f1

def bleu(ref_tokens, hyp_tokens, max_n=4):
    ref_len, hyp_len = len(ref_tokens), len(hyp_tokens)
    if hyp_len == 0:
        return 0.0
    bp = 1.0 if hyp_len > ref_len else math.exp(1 - ref_len / hyp_len)
    log_avg, eps_used = 0.0, False
    precisions = []
    for n in range(1, max_n + 1):
        ref_ng, hyp_ng = ngrams(ref_tokens, n), ngrams(hyp_tokens, n)
        clipped = sum(min(c, ref_ng.get(g, 0)) for g, c in hyp_ng.items())
        total = sum(hyp_ng.values())
        p = clipped / total if total else 0.0
        if p == 0.0:
            p, eps_used = 1e-9, True
        precisions.append(p)
        log_avg += math.log(p)
    bleu_score = bp * math.exp(log_avg / max_n)
    return bleu_score, precisions, eps_used

def fact_coverage(text):
    norm = normalize(text)
    covered, missing = [], []
    for label, alts in FACTS:
        if any(all(needle in norm for needle in alt) for alt in alts):
            covered.append(label)
        else:
            missing.append(label)
    return covered, missing

def topic_coverage(text):
    norm = normalize(text)
    return [t for t in TOPICS if t in norm]

def syllables(word):
    w = word.lower()
    if len(w) <= 3:
        return 1
    w = re.sub(r"(?:es|ed|e)$", "", w)
    return max(1, len(re.findall(r"[aeiouy]+", w)))

def readability(text):
    words = re.findall(r"[a-z']+", text.lower())
    sents = max(1, len(re.findall(r"[.!?]+", text)))
    nw, nsyl = len(words), sum(syllables(w) for w in words)
    if nw == 0:
        return 0.0, 0.0
    flesch = 206.835 - 1.015 * (nw / sents) - 84.6 * (nsyl / nw)
    fk = 0.39 * (nw / sents) + 11.8 * (nsyl / nw) - 15.59
    return flesch, fk

def evaluate(name, text, ref_text, ref_tokens):
    tokens = tokenize(text)
    r1 = rouge_n(ref_tokens, tokens, 1)
    r2 = rouge_n(ref_tokens, tokens, 2)
    rl = rouge_l(ref_tokens, tokens)
    b, precs, smoothed = bleu(ref_tokens, tokens)
    covered, missing = fact_coverage(text)
    topics = topic_coverage(text)
    flesch, fk = readability(text)
    return {
        "name": name,
        "words": len(tokens),
        "compression": round(len(tokens) / len(ref_tokens) * 100, 1),
        "rouge1": r1, "rouge2": r2, "rougeL": rl,
        "bleu": b, "bleu_precs": precs, "bleu_smoothed": smoothed,
        "facts_covered": len(covered), "facts_total": len(FACTS),
        "covered": covered, "missing": missing,
        "topics": topics, "flesch": flesch, "fk_grade": fk,
    }

def fmt_rpf(t):
    return f"R={t[0]:.3f} P={t[1]:.3f} F={t[2]:.3f}"

def main():
    texts = {k: read(v) for k, v in PATHS.items()}
    ref_text, ref_tokens = texts["article"], tokenize(texts["article"])

    results = {
        "gpt4": evaluate("GPT-4", texts["gpt4"], ref_text, ref_tokens),
        "claude": evaluate("Claude", texts["claude"], ref_text, ref_tokens),
    }

    print("=" * 78)
    print("SUMMARY EVALUATION REPORT  (reference = article.txt)")
    print("=" * 78)

    # 1) Length / compression
    print("\n[1] LENGTH / COMPRESSION")
    for r in results.values():
        print(f"  {r['name']:<8} words={r['words']:>4}  compression={r['compression']:>5.1f}% of article")

    # 2) ROUGE
    print("\n[2] ROUGE (overlap with source article; higher = more source content retained)")
    print(f"  {'model':<8} {'ROUGE-1':<26} {'ROUGE-2':<26} {'ROUGE-L':<26}")
    for r in results.values():
        print(f"  {r['name']:<8} {fmt_rpf(r['rouge1']):<26} {fmt_rpf(r['rouge2']):<26} {fmt_rpf(r['rougeL']):<26}")

    # 3) BLEU
    print("\n[3] BLEU vs source (lexical n-gram overlap; translation-oriented, informational only)")
    for r in results.values():
        p1, p2, p3, p4 = r["bleu_precs"]
        print(f"  {r['name']:<8} BLEU={r['bleu']:.4f}  p1={p1:.3f} p2={p2:.3f} p3={p3:.3f} p4={p4:.3f}"
              + ("  (smoothed)" if r["bleu_smoothed"] else ""))

    # 4) Fact retention
    print(f"\n[4] FACT RETENTION (custom groundedness check, {len(FACTS)} key facts from article)")
    for r in results.values():
        print(f"  {r['name']:<8} retained {r['facts_covered']}/{r['facts_total']} facts")
        print(f"           retained: {', '.join(r['covered']) if r['covered'] else '(none)'}")
        print(f"           missing:   {', '.join(r['missing']) if r['missing'] else '(none)'}")

    # 5) Topic coverage
    print("\n[5] TOPIC COVERAGE (section-level)")
    for r in results.values():
        print(f"  {r['name']:<8} {len(r['topics'])}/{len(TOPICS)} topics: {', '.join(r['topics'])}")

    # 6) Readability (descriptive only)
    print("\n[6] READABILITY (descriptive; not a quality score)")
    for r in results.values():
        print(f"  {r['name']:<8} Flesch Reading Ease={r['flesch']:.1f}  Flesch-Kincaid grade={r['fk_grade']:.1f}")

    # 7) Head-to-head
    print("\n[7] HEAD-TO-HEAD")
    g, c = results["gpt4"], results["claude"]
    rows = [
        ("ROUGE-1 F1", g["rouge1"][2], c["rouge1"][2], "higher is better"),
        ("ROUGE-2 F1", g["rouge2"][2], c["rouge2"][2], "higher is better"),
        ("ROUGE-L F1", g["rougeL"][2], c["rougeL"][2], "higher is better"),
        ("BLEU", g["bleu"], c["bleu"], "higher is better"),
        ("Facts retained", g["facts_covered"], c["facts_covered"], "higher is better"),
        ("Compression %", g["compression"], c["compression"], "descriptive"),
    ]
    for label, a, b, note in rows:
        winner = "Claude" if b > a else ("GPT-4" if a > b else "tie")
        print(f"  {label:<16} GPT-4={a:<10.4g} Claude={b:<10.4g} -> {winner}  ({note})")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
